query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys, high-temperature oxidation resistance is governed by differential elemental diffusion that leads to the in-situ formation of a self-healing, adherent oxide scale enriched in refractory and low-diffusivity elements.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized (solution-treated) multiprincipal-element alloy with a uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled high-temperature oxidation experiments (800–1200 °C) on alloys with standard composition and on variants engineered with increased fractions of refractory/glassy oxide‐forming elements (e.g., added Ta). Complement the experiments with simulation-driven analysis of elemental diffusion and interfacial reaction kinetics.
generation.conditions: Exposure to controlled oxidizing atmospheres at temperatures between 800 °C and 1200 °C, including both constant temperature and cyclic oxidation protocols over extended durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a protective oxide layer (passive scale) that is selectively enriched in refractory, slow-diffusing elements and may incorporate glass-forming species, resulting in a dense and viscous barrier against oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: Differential diffusion at high temperature causes elements with inherently lower mobility (e.g., Ta or similar refractory elements) to segregate at the alloy surface. Their oxidation produces a stable, adherent passive oxide that significantly slows further oxidation and preserves the alloy’s bulk integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys engineered to enhance the content of refractory/glassy oxide-formers will form thinner, more uniform, and adherent oxide scales, exhibit reduced weight gain, and better retain mechanical properties compared to baseline alloys lacking these modifications.
generation.baseline: Standard multiprincipal-element alloys without targeted compositional adjustments to favor slow-diffusing, protective oxide-forming elements.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic relationship is expected to be valid over the high-temperature range of 800–1200 °C. Deviations may occur outside this range due to different oxidation kinetics or phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative influence of individual elemental diffusion rates, the exact oxide phase compositions, and their interplay require further calibration. Simulation predictions must be iteratively refined with experimental measurements to fully delineate the parameter space.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sample sets: one set of baseline multiprincipal-element alloys and another set modified with additional refractory/glassy oxide-forming elements (e.g., increased Ta content). Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation in a controlled furnace at 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C under identical oxidizing conditions, using both isothermal and cyclic protocols. Simultaneously, perform simulation studies to predict elemental diffusion profiles and oxide scale formation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (using SEM and TEM)
Phase composition of oxide scales (using HTXRD and EDS)
Weight gain per unit area during oxidation
Retention of mechanical properties post-oxidation (via nanoindentation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloys do not show a significantly reduced oxide thickness, lower weight gain, and better mechanical property retention compared to the baseline, or if the observed elemental segregation and oxide scale composition do not correlate with the predicted slow-diffusion of refractory elements, then the hypothesis that differential elemental diffusion governs oxidation resistance is falsified.

High-entropy boride (HEB) ceramics combine ultra-high melting points, superior hardness, and compositional tunability, enabling service in extreme environments; however, difficult densification and limited fracture toughness still constrain their aerospace applications. In this study, metallic Ta was introduced into high-entropy (Ti0.2Zr0.2Hf0.2Nb0.2Ta0.2)B2 as both a sintering aid and a toughening phase. Bulk HEB-Ta composites were fabricated by spark plasma sintering to investigate the effect of Ta content on densification behavior, microstructure, mechanical properties, and high-temperature oxidation resistance. The results show that an appropriate amount of Ta markedly promotes densification; at 10 vol% Ta, the open porosity reaches a minimum of 0.15%. Hardness and fracture toughness exhibit an increase-then-decrease trend with Ta content, attaining maxima at 15 vol% Ta (20.79 ± 0.17 GPa and 4.31 ± 0.12 MPa·, respectively). During oxidation at 800–1400 °C, the extent of oxidation increases with temperature, yet the composite with 10 vol% Ta shows the best oxidation resistance. At oxidation temperatures between 1000 and 1200 °C, the diffraction peak intensities increase overall, the number of phase types increases, and more solid solution phases such as Ta and Nb are formed. This suggests that higher temperatures promote a more complete oxidation reaction, leading to the formation of additional phases and an increase in crystallinity. At 1400 °C, the diffraction peaks tend to broaden, due to enhanced grain growth and intensified diffusion reactions between phases at high temperature. Although the phase types remain consistent with those at medium temperatures, the crystalline state changes due to high-temperature kinetics.

frame.system: Multiprincipal-element alloys (e.g., high‐entropy alloys) that are designed to operate in harsh, high-temperature, oxidizing environments, starting from a homogenized or solution‐treated state.
frame.goal: To identify and validate the dominant mechanistic pathway that governs oxidation resistance and overall material integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
frame.limitation: Current understanding is limited in pinpointing the detailed mechanism(s) by which these complex alloys resist oxidation and degradation under sustained high-temperature conditions.
root_cause_cues: sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments
constraints: Hypothesis must be testable via controlled comparison experiments.
Observations must be interpretable relative to a defined baseline.
The hypothesis should hold over a specified temperature (and possibly compositional) range.
The design should reveal not only improved performance but also enough mechanistic insight to differentiate competing hypotheses.
frame.regime: High-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 800–1200 °C) in controlled oxidizing atmospheres over sustained durations, possibly including cyclic oxidation to simulate real-use conditions.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have employed bulk oxidation tests and post-mortem scale characterization that provided only phenomenological correlations.
Attempts to correlate individual element volatility or diffusion rates with oxidation resistance have fallen short in establishing a clear, predictive mechanistic model.
